title: Truth, Tricks and Trouble
summary: People used to say the camera never lies, but people behind cameras sometimes do. In this part you will meet ghost photos, paper fairies and leaders who made enemies vanish from pictures. You will also see how cameras raised hard questions about privacy, safety and fairness, and how honest photos helped make the world better.

sections.heading: Ghosts in the Darkroom
paragraphs: Imagine walking into a photography studio in Boston in the early 1860s. The country is at war, and many families have lost someone. A photographer named William H. Mumler makes you an offer: sit for your portrait, and the camera may also capture the spirit of a loved one who has died. A few days later you collect your print. There you are, sitting stiffly in a chair, and floating behind you is a pale, misty face. For a grieving person, that picture could feel like a miracle.

Mumler (1832 to 1884) was the most famous 'spirit photographer' of his time. According to his own story, his first ghost picture happened by accident. He took a self-portrait and, when he developed it, he said a faint figure appeared beside him, which he claimed was a cousin who had died 12 years earlier. Whether that first image was a mistake or a plan, Mumler soon realized that people would pay well for portraits with ghosts in them.

Today we know how such pictures could be made. Remember from earlier parts that a glass negative records whatever light reaches it. If a photographer exposes the same plate twice, once with a person dressed up as a pale 'spirit' and once with the paying customer, both images end up layered on top of each other. This is called a double exposure. A photographer could also slip in a prepared plate that already carried a faint image. Because most customers had no idea how photography worked, the results looked mysterious.

Mumler's most famous picture appears to show Mary Todd Lincoln, the widow of President Abraham Lincoln, with the shadowy figure of her husband standing behind her, his hands resting on her shoulders. Historians give different dates for it, from about 1869 to the early 1870s. Most experts consider it a double exposure, but it became one of the best-known spirit photographs ever made.

Not everyone was fooled. Some customers recognized the 'ghosts' in their pictures as people who were still very much alive. In April 1869, Mumler was put on trial in New York for fraud. One of the witnesses against him was the famous showman P. T. Barnum, a man who knew a lot about entertaining tricks. Barnum argued that Mumler was taking advantage of grieving people. To prove how easy it was, Barnum had another photographer, Abraham Bogardus, make a picture of Barnum himself with the 'ghost' of Abraham Lincoln. The fake was shown in court.

Surprisingly, Mumler was found not guilty. The prosecution could not prove beyond doubt exactly how he had faked his pictures. Even so, his story taught an early lesson that still matters: a photograph can look completely real and still be a trick. Spirit photography stayed popular for decades, especially after the huge losses of the First World War, when many families again longed for comfort.

sections.heading: Fairies at the Bottom of the Garden
paragraphs: In 1917, in the village of Cottingley near Bradford in the north of England, two cousins spent their days playing by a small stream, which locals call a beck, at the bottom of the garden. Elsie Wright was 16, and Frances Griffiths was 9. Frances kept coming home with wet feet, and when the grown-ups scolded her, the girls said they had been playing with fairies.

Elsie borrowed her father Arthur's camera, a small plate camera called a Midg, and the girls went down to the beck. When Arthur, an amateur photographer, developed the plate, he saw Frances leaning on her hand while a group of tiny winged fairies danced in front of her. A later photo showed Elsie holding out her hand to a small gnome. Arthur suspected the fairies were paper cut-outs and would not lend the camera again. Elsie's mother, Polly, was more curious.

In 1919, Polly took the photos to a meeting of the Theosophical Society, a group interested in spiritual ideas. A member named Edward Gardner became excited and began showing the pictures at his lectures. Experts gave mixed opinions. A photographer named Harold Snelling said he could find no sign the negatives had been tampered with. Kodak declined to say the pictures were genuine, and the Ilford company reported some evidence of faking.

Then the story reached one of the most famous writers in the world: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes. Isn't it strange that the man who invented the world's most logical detective was fooled? Conan Doyle believed strongly in spiritualism, the idea that the living can contact spirits, and he hoped that if people accepted fairies, they might be more open to other unseen things. In December 1920, he published the photos in The Strand Magazine. To protect the girls, the article called them 'Alice' and 'Iris'.

Earlier, in the summer of 1920, Gardner gave the cousins two cameras and 24 plates that he had secretly marked, so that no one could swap them. The girls produced three more fairy photos that summer, bringing the total to five. The pictures caused a sensation, and arguments about them carried on for more than 60 years.

Finally, in 1983, the cousins, now elderly women, admitted the truth in a magazine called The Unexplained. Elsie had copied fairy drawings from a popular children's book, Princess Mary's Gift Book, cut them out of cardboard, and held them up with hatpins. One mystery remained: Frances always insisted that the fifth photo was real, while Elsie said it was faked, and both claimed to have taken it. Both women also said, to the end, that they really had seen fairies by the beck.

Why did so many adults believe two girls with paper cut-outs? Partly because they wanted to. After years of war, the idea of a magical world felt hopeful. And partly because many people trusted photographs more than their own common sense. The prints and the cameras are kept today at the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford, a reminder of how a simple trick can fool even a very clever person.

sections.heading: Scissors, Paint and Vanishing People
paragraphs: Some people think photo editing began with computers. In fact, it is nearly as old as photography itself. Back in 1840, Hippolyte Bayard staged his own fake death in a photo to complain about not getting credit for his invention, as you read in Part 5. In 1857, the Swedish-born photographer Oscar Rejlander created a large artwork called The Two Ways of Life by combining about 30 separate negatives into one print, like a jigsaw puzzle. A well-known portrait of Abraham Lincoln from the 1860s turns out to be Lincoln's head attached to the body of another politician, John C. Calhoun.

Even war photos were sometimes arranged. In 1863, after the Battle of Gettysburg, Alexander Gardner's team photographed a fallen soldier lying among rocks, in a scene titled Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter. More than a hundred years later, historian William Frassanito studied the landscape closely and argued that the same body appears in another photo taken some distance away, so it seems the photographers moved it to make a more dramatic picture. Early photographers often did not think of this as lying. They thought of themselves as making a powerful picture, not a scientific record.

The most chilling photo editing happened in the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin, who ruled from the 1920s until 1953. Stalin had many former allies arrested and killed. It was not enough for them to disappear from life; they also had to disappear from history. Workers in photo departments used airbrushes, tiny paint sprayers, along with retouching paint, scalpels and careful rephotography to remove people from pictures.

The best-known example involves Nikolai Yezhov. He was the head of the Soviet secret police during the worst years of Stalin's purges, a time when huge numbers of people were arrested. In one photo, Yezhov walks beside Stalin along the bank of the Moscow-Volga Canal. Then Yezhov himself fell from power. He was arrested in 1939 and executed in 1940. In later versions of the photograph, he is simply gone. Where he once stood, there is only water and stone, as if Stalin had been strolling alone with his other companions.

Yezhov was not the only one. A famous photo shows Vladimir Lenin speaking to soldiers in Moscow on 5 May 1920, with Leon Trotsky and Lev Kamenev standing on the steps beside the platform. After Trotsky and Kamenev fell out of favor, they were painted out of the picture. Even a cosmonaut trainee named Valentin Bondarenko, who died in a training accident in 1961, was removed from group photos, and the public did not learn he had existed until 1986. The British writer and designer David King collected many before-and-after examples in a book called The Commissar Vanishes (1997).

Moving pictures could be used to shape people's beliefs, too. Films made to persuade people, often by governments, are called propaganda films. In the 1930s, Nazi Germany used carefully staged films such as Leni Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will (1935) to make its leader look all-powerful and its huge rallies look magnificent. Many countries, including Britain and the United States, made propaganda films during the Second World War as well. The lesson for viewers was the same as for photos: a film shows what its makers chose to film, frame and keep.

sections.heading: Whose Picture Is It, Anyway?
paragraphs: As cameras became smaller and faster, a new worry appeared: being photographed without saying yes. You may remember from Part 9 that in 1890 two American lawyers, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis, wrote an article called The Right to Privacy, partly because snapshot cameras and gossip newspapers made it easy to publish pictures of people's private lives. That worry has only grown since.

In 1960, the Italian director Federico Fellini made a film called La Dolce Vita, which includes a pushy news photographer named Paparazzo who chases celebrities around Rome. His name became a word. Today, 'paparazzi' (the plural) means photographers who follow famous people to snap candid pictures and sell them to magazines and websites. Some celebrities fought back in court. In the United States, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, the widow of President John F. Kennedy, won a court order in the 1970s that kept the photographer Ron Galella a set distance away from her and her children.

The most painful example came in 1997, when Diana, Princess of Wales, died in a car crash in a tunnel in Paris while her driver was speeding away from photographers. Official investigations blamed mainly the driver's speed and his drinking, but the tragedy made many people around the world ask whether chasing someone for a photo had gone too far. Later, some places passed laws to protect people, especially children. In 2013, for example, California passed a law against harassing children because of who their parents are, including to photograph them.

Cameras also began to watch everyone, not only the famous. Closed-circuit television, or CCTV, means cameras that send pictures to a limited set of screens rather than broadcasting to the public. One early system was installed in Germany in 1942 to watch rocket launches from a safe distance. In 1968, the town of Olean, New York, became the first city in the United States to put video cameras along its main shopping street to fight crime. The United Kingdom became famous for its many cameras; estimates of the number range from under 2 million to more than 4 million, depending on how they are counted.

Supporters say such cameras help solve crimes and keep people safe. Critics worry that being watched all the time, especially when cameras can be linked to computers that recognize faces, takes away people's freedom to go about their lives without being tracked. Many countries now have rules about where cameras can point, how long recordings may be kept and who may look at them.

There is one more puzzle: if someone takes a photo of you, who owns it? In many countries, the copyright, meaning the legal right to copy and sell a creative work, usually belongs to the person who pressed the button, not the person in the picture. But laws differ. In some places, using a person's photo in an advertisement without permission is not allowed, and many schools and websites ask parents before sharing pictures of children. A good rule for everyone, at any age: ask before you post a picture of someone else.

sections.heading: Smoke at the Hogmanay Matinee
paragraphs: Some of photography's troubles were not about truth at all, but about safety. For decades, movie film was made from cellulose nitrate, the clear, bright plastic you met in Part 11. Nitrate gave sharp, beautiful pictures, but it had a terrible secret. It burns extremely fast, and because the material contains oxygen in its own chemical makeup, a nitrate fire can keep burning even when it is covered up, and can produce thick, poisonous smoke.

On the afternoon of 31 December 1929, the last day of the year, which Scots call Hogmanay, hundreds of children packed into the Glen Cinema in Paisley, a town near Glasgow in Scotland, for a special matinee. Estimates say there were between 700 and 1,000 children, from toddlers to about 14 years old. For many of them, a cheap holiday picture show was a special treat.

During the show, a canister of film that had been placed in a small room near the projection area began to give off thick smoke. An official inquiry later concluded that the canister had been set down on a battery and that an electrical short circuit started it smoldering. A young assistant tried to smother it, but the canister came open and smoke drifted into the hall where the children sat. There were no big flames in the auditorium, but someone shouted 'Fire!' and the children rushed for the exits.

What happened next was a crush, not a fire. One of the escape doors at the bottom of a stairway opened inward and had been padlocked shut. As frightened children pushed forward, those at the front could not get out, and more children piled up behind them. Seventy-one children died, mostly from being crushed or unable to breathe, and dozens more were hurt. The cinema's manager was put on trial but was found not guilty. Since 2009, the town has held a memorial service every year.

The disaster changed the rules for cinemas across Britain. The law was strengthened to require more exits, doors that open outward, push bars that can be opened easily in a hurry, and limits on how many people a theater can hold. Next time you see a long metal bar across a cinema or school exit door, you are looking at a safety idea shaped by tragedies like this one. Nitrate film itself was gradually replaced by much safer 'safety film', and by the early 1950s new film stock was no longer made of nitrate.

Photography caused another quieter kind of harm: pollution. Making and developing film used large amounts of chemicals, including silver compounds, acids and strong solvents. For many years, some factories and photo labs released waste into rivers, sewers and the air. Silver can harm fish and other water life, and some solvents are bad for people to breathe. Over the late 20th century, governments tightened environmental laws, and labs learned to capture and recycle silver from their used chemicals. Digital cameras removed most darkroom chemicals, though they bring their own problem: mountains of electronic waste.

sections.heading: Whose Skin Did the Film See?
paragraphs: Here is a kind of unfairness that is hard to spot because it is built right into the machines. When you get photos printed from film, the printing lab has to decide how to balance the colors. Too much red, and everyone looks sunburned; too much blue, and everyone looks chilly. To check their machines, labs in North America used reference cards showing a photo of a woman next to colored patches and gray scales. These cards became known as Shirley cards, reportedly after one of the first models to pose for them.

For decades, the woman on the standard card was a light-skinned white woman. Labs adjusted their equipment so that her skin looked 'right'. The film chemistry itself had also been developed with light skin in mind. The result was that people with darker skin were often photographed poorly. Their faces could come out too dark, lacking detail, or with a strange color, especially when they stood next to lighter-skinned friends in the same picture. Many families of color have old school photos where faces look like dark shadows.

The Canadian researcher Lorna Roth, who studied this history, found that some of the first pressure to improve film came from an unexpected direction. Companies that sold chocolate and dark wooden furniture complained that the film could not show the rich differences between dark browns in their advertisements. During the 1970s and 1980s, film makers including Kodak improved their films so they could record a wider range of dark tones. In the mid-1990s, Kodak introduced a new reference card showing three women with different skin colors.

The story of the Shirley card matters because it shows that technology is not automatically neutral. A machine is tested on whatever examples its designers choose. If those examples include only some kinds of people, the machine may work worse for everyone else. The same question comes up today with digital cameras, face-recognition software and AI programs. Engineers now often test camera sensors and software on a wide range of skin tones, and some phone makers advertise cameras designed to show all skin tones accurately. Asking 'who was this tested on?' is one of the smartest questions a young inventor can learn.

sections.heading: Rules for the Silver Screen
paragraphs: Movies faced their own battles over what could be shown. In the 1920s, a string of Hollywood scandals and pressure from local censor boards worried the big studios. Rather than have dozens of governments cutting their films, the studios decided to police themselves. Their trade group was led by Will H. Hays, and in 1930 it adopted a set of rules called the Motion Picture Production Code, often known as the Hays Code.

At first many filmmakers ignored it. But starting in 1934, a new office called the Production Code Administration, led by Joseph Breen, enforced it strictly. A film needed the office's seal of approval to be shown in most major theaters. The rules said criminals must always be punished by the end, that authority figures like police and clergy must be treated with respect, and that bad language and many adult subjects were not allowed. Some rules were openly unjust: the code banned showing a romance between a Black person and a white person.

Hollywood also spread hurtful stereotypes, meaning unfair, oversimplified pictures of whole groups of people. Black actors were mostly offered roles as servants or comic characters. When Hattie McDaniel became the first African American to win an Academy Award, in 1940 for Gone with the Wind, she had to sit at a separate table at the ceremony. The Chinese American star Anna May Wong hoped to play the lead in The Good Earth (1937), a story set in China, but the role went to a white actress, Luise Rainer, wearing makeup to look Asian. One biographer believed the code's rules about romance were part of the reason, though other historians are not sure. Native American characters were often shown as nothing but villains in westerns.

These things were challenged from the start. Groups such as the NAACP, the oldest civil rights organization in the United States, protested racist films. Independent Black filmmakers such as Oscar Micheaux made dozens of films from 1919 onward with Black casts telling their own stories. Over time, actors, writers and audiences pushed for fairer and more truthful portrayals, and the work continues today.

The code itself slowly lost its grip. Television, foreign films and bold directors pushed against it. A 1952 Supreme Court decision said films deserved free speech protection, and the comedy Some Like It Hot was released without a seal in 1959 and was a hit anyway. On 1 November 1968, the code was replaced by a rating system with letters that told audiences, especially parents, what to expect, rather than banning subjects altogether. Today's movie ratings come from that idea.

sections.heading: When Pictures Tell the Truth
paragraphs: After all these tricks and troubles, you might wonder whether we should trust photos at all. The answer is yes, but wisely. Honest photographs have changed the world for the better again and again.

You met Lewis Hine in Part 16. His pictures of children working in mills and mines gave Americans evidence they could not ignore and helped support laws against child labor. In 1955, after a 14-year-old Black boy named Emmett Till was murdered in Mississippi, his mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, chose to let the world see what had been done to her son. Photographs published in Jet magazine shocked many Americans and helped energize the civil rights movement. Photos of polluted rivers, starving families and damaged forests have led to laws, rescues and donations.

Photos are also the backbone of science. In 1952, a photograph made using X-rays in the lab of Rosalind Franklin, known as Photo 51, helped scientists work out the double-helix shape of DNA. Astronomers use photos to discover planets and measure the universe. Doctors use images to find broken bones and diseases. In all these cases, scientists record exactly how a picture was made, so others can check it.

And photos are memory. A family album lets you see your great-grandparents' faces; a class photo freezes a year of your life. Museums and archives collect photos carefully, recording who took them, when and where. That information, called provenance, is how historians tell a real record from a fake.

So how can you be a good photo detective? Ask who took the picture, and why. Look for the original source. Check whether other photos or witnesses show the same thing. Notice what might be outside the frame. A photo is not truth or lies by itself; it is a piece of evidence, and like all evidence it has to be checked.

Meanwhile, while people argued about fake fairies and studio censors, the movie theater was facing a brand-new rival. In 1948, only about 1 out of every 100 American homes had a television set. By 1955, about three out of four did. A glowing box in the living room was about to change how everyone watched moving pictures.

deepDive: Historians of photography argue less about whether old photos were manipulated (many were) than about what counts as manipulation. In the 1800s, combination printing, retouching negatives with pencil, and adding clouds from a separate negative were normal studio practice, because early plates could not record bright skies and dark land at the same time. Was a photographer lying by adding clouds, or correcting a technical limitation? Today, news agencies usually draw a line: adjusting brightness and contrast is acceptable, but adding, removing or moving things is not. The debate over staging is just as lively. William Frassanito's work on Gettysburg photos in the 1970s showed that at least one body was moved for Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter, while the authenticity of Robert Capa's 1936 photo The Falling Soldier, from the Spanish Civil War, is still argued over, with some researchers suggesting it was taken away from the actual fighting. Soviet retouching is a different category: it was systematic, ordered by the state and meant to rewrite the record. Its tools, from airbrushes to rephotographing pasted-up prints, were slow, so investigators can often detect them by looking for blurred edges, mismatched grain and impossible shadows. The Cottingley case shows a third problem: experts at the time tested whether the negatives had been altered, and they had not. The fakery happened in front of the lens, not in the darkroom, so a 'genuine' negative could still record a lie. Bias in film, such as the Shirley card standard, is subtler still, because no one has to intend to deceive for a picture to misrepresent someone. Researchers like Lorna Roth argue that technical standards carry the assumptions of the people who set them. Modern answers include forensic software that checks for copied pixels, metadata that records camera settings, and newer 'content credentials' that try to log every edit. None is perfect, which is why historians still rely on the oldest method of all: comparing many independent sources.
funFact: In the 1860s, the showman P. T. Barnum had a fake 'spirit photograph' made of himself with the ghost of Abraham Lincoln, just to prove in court how easy such pictures were to fake.
